entries.7c760095e628d573f5078088fa1a7dca5583ea11: <div sID="gen20109" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Amos.3" sID="Amos.3"/> <div eID="gen20109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20110" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20111" type="x-p"/> A stupid, senseless, heedless people, are, in this chapter, called upon to take notice, I. Of the judgments of God denounced against them and the warnings he gave them of those judgments, and to be hereby awakened out of their security, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.1-Amos.3.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. II. Of the sins that were found among them, by which God was provoked thus to threaten, thus to punish, that they might justify God in his controversy with them, and, unless they repented and reformed, might expect no other than that God should proceed in his controversy, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.9-Amos.3.15">ver. 9-15</reference>.
entries.131b8541edec491da49e6949d96492201882aa3d: <div eID="gen20111" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20110" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Remonstrance with Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 790.)</title> <div sID="gen20112" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Hear this word that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoken against you, O children of Israel, against the whole family which I brought up from the land of Egypt, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> You only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities. <hi type="super">3</hi> Can two walk together, except they be agreed? <hi type="super">4</hi> Will a lion roar in the forest, when he hath no prey? will a young lion cry out of his den, if he have taken nothing? <hi type="super">5</hi> Can a bird fall in a snare upon the earth, where no gin <hi type="italic">is</hi> for him? shall <hi type="italic">one</hi> take up a snare from the earth, and have taken nothing at all? <hi type="super">6</hi> Shall a trumpet be blown in the city, and the people not be afraid? shall there be evil in a city, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath not done <hi type="italic">it?</hi> <hi type="super">7</hi> Surely the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets. <hi type="super">8</hi> The lion hath roared, who will not fear? the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> hath spoken, who can but prophesy? <div eID="gen20112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20113" type="x-p"/> The scope of these verses is to convince the people of Israel that God had a controversy with them. That which the prophet has to say to them is to let them know that the Lord has something to say against them, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.1">v. 1</reference>. They were his peculiar people above others, knew his name, and were called by it; <hi type="italic">nevertheless he had something against them,</hi> and they were called to hear what it was, that they might consider what answer they should make, as the prisoner at the bar is told to hearken to his indictment. The <hi type="italic">children of Israel</hi> would not regard the words of counsel and comfort that God had many a time spoken to them, and now they shall be made to hear the word of reproof and threatening that the Lord has spoken against them; for he will act as he has spoken. <div eID="gen20113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20114" type="x-p"/> I. Let them know that the gracious cognizance God has taken of them, and the favours he has bestowed upon them, should not exempt them from the punishment due to them for their sins. Israel is a <hi type="italic">family</hi> that <hi type="italic">God brought up out of the land of Egypt,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.1">v. 1</reference>), and it was no more than a family when it went down thither; thence God delivered it; thence he fetched it to be a family to himself. It is not only the ten tribes, the kingdom of Israel, that must take notice of this, but that of Judah also, for it is spoken against the whole <hi type="italic">family</hi> that God <hi type="italic">brought up out of Egypt.</hi> It is a family that God has bestowed distinguishing favours upon, has owned in a peculiar manner. <hi type="italic">You only have I known of all the families of the earth.</hi> Note, God's church in the world is a family dignified above all the families of the earth. Those that know God are known of him. <hi type="italic">In Judah is God known,</hi> and therefore Judah is more than any people known of God. God has <hi type="italic">known</hi> them, that is, he has chosen them, covenanted with them, and conversed with them as his acquaintance. Now, one would think, it should follow, "Therefore I will spare you, will connive at your faults, and excuse you." No: <hi type="italic">Therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.</hi> Note, The distinguishing favours of God to us, if they do not serve to restrain us from sin, shall not serve to exempt us from punishment; nay, the nearer any are to God in profession, and the kinder notice he has taken of them, the more surely, the more quickly, and the more severely will he reckon with them, if they by a course of wilful sin profane their character, disgrace their relation to him, violate their engagements, and put a slight upon the favours and honours with which they have been distinguished. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> they shall be punished, because their sins dishonour him, affront him, and grieve him, more than the sins of others, and because it is necessary that God should vindicate his own honour by making it appear that he hates sin and hates it most in those that are nearest to him; if they be but as bad as others, they shall be punished worse than others, because it is justly expected that they should be so much better than others. <hi type="italic">Judgment begins at the house of God,</hi> begins at the sanctuary; for God will be sanctified either by or upon those that <hi type="italic">come nigh unto him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.10.3">Lev. x. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen20114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20115" type="x-p"/> II. Let them know that they could not expect any comfortable communion with God unless they first made their peace with him (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Can two walk together except they be agreed?</hi> No; how should they? Where there is not friendship there can be no fellowship; if two persons be at variance, they must first accommodate the matters in difference between them before there can be any interchanging of good offices. Israel has affronted God, had broken their covenant with him, and ill-requited his favours to them; and yet they expected that he should continue to walk with them, should take their part, act for them, and give them assurances of his presence with them, though they took no care by repentance and reformation to <hi type="italic">agree with their adversary</hi> and to turn away his wrath. "But how can that be?" says God. "While you continue to <hi type="italic">walk contrary to God</hi> you can look for no other than that he should <hi type="italic">walk contrary to you,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Lev.26.23-Lev.26.24">Lev. xxvi. 23, 24</reference>. Note, We cannot expect that God should be present with us, or act for us, unless we be reconciled to him. God and man cannot <hi type="italic">walk together except they be agreed.</hi> Unless we agree with God in our end, which is his glory, we cannot walk with him by the way. <div eID="gen20115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20116" type="x-p"/> III. Let them know that the warnings God gave them of judgments approaching were not causeless and groundless, merely to amuse them, but certain declarations of the wrath of God against them, which (if they did not speedily repent) they would infallibly feel the effects of (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Will a lion roar in the forest when he has no prey</hi> in view? No: he roars upon his prey. Nor will a <hi type="italic">young lion cry out of his den</hi> if the old lion <hi type="italic">have taken nothing</hi> to bring home to him; nor would God thus give you warning both by the threatenings of his word, and by less judgments, if you had not by your sins made yourselves a prey to his wrath, nor if he were not really about to fall upon you with desolating destroying judgments." Note, The threatenings of the word and providence of God are not bugbears, to frighten children and fools, but are certain inferences from the sin of man and certain presages of the judgments of God. <div eID="gen20116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20117" type="x-p"/> IV. Let them know that, as their own wickedness was the procuring cause of these judgments, so they shall not be removed till they have done their work, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.5">v. 5</reference>. When God has come forth to contend with a sinful people it is necessary that they should understand, 1. That it is their own sin that has entangled them; for <hi type="italic">can a bird fall in a snare upon the earth where no gin is for him?</hi> No, nature does not lay snares for the creatures, but the art of men; a bird is not taken in a snare by chance, but with the fowler's design; so the providence of God prepares trouble for sinners, and it is <hi type="italic">in the work of their own hands</hi> that they <hi type="italic">are snared.</hi> Affliction does not <hi type="italic">spring out of the dust,</hi> but it is God's justice, and <hi type="italic">our own wickedness,</hi> that <hi type="italic">correct us.</hi> 2. It is nothing but their own repentance that can disentangle them; for <hi type="italic">shall one take up a snare from the earth,</hi> which he laid with design, except he have <hi type="italic">taken something</hi> as he designed? So neither will God remove the affliction he has sent till it have done its work and accomplished that for which he sent it. If our hearts be duly humbled, and we are brought by our afflictions to confess and forsake our sins, then the snare has taken something, then the point is gained, the end is answered, and then, and not till then, the <hi type="italic">snare is broken,</hi> is taken up from the earth, and <hi type="italic">we are delivered</hi> in love and mercy. <div eID="gen20117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20118" type="x-p"/> V. Let them know that all their troubles came from the hand of God's providence and from the counsel of his will (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Shall there be evil in a city,</hi> in a family, in a nation, <hi type="italic">and the Lord has not done it,</hi> appointed it, and performed what he appointed? The evil of sin is from ourselves; it is our own doing. But the evil of trouble, personal or public, is from God, and is his doing; whoever are the instruments, God is the principal agent. <hi type="italic">Out of his mouth both evil and good proceed.</hi> This consideration, that, whatever evil is in the city, the Lord has done it, should engage us patiently to bear our share in public calamities and to study to answer God's intention in them. <div eID="gen20118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20119" type="x-p"/> VI. Let them know that their prophets, who give them warning of judgments approaching, deliver nothing to them but what they have <hi type="italic">received from the Lord</hi> to be delivered to his people. 1. God makes it known beforehand to the prophets (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Surely the Lord Jehovah will do nothing,</hi> none of that evil in the city spoken of (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">but he reveals it to his servants the prophets,</hi> though to others it is a secret. Therefore those know not what they do who make light of the warnings which the prophets give them, in God's name. Observe, God's prophets are <hi type="italic">his servants,</hi> whom he employs to go on his errands to the children of men. The <hi type="italic">secret</hi> of God is with them; it is in some sense with all <hi type="italic">the righteous</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.32">Prov. iii. 32</reference>), with <hi type="italic">all that fear God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.14">Ps. xxv. 14</reference>), but in a peculiar manner with the prophets, to whom the Spirit of prophecy is a Spirit of revelation. It would have put honour enough upon prophets if it had been only said that sometimes God is pleased to reveal to his prophets what he designs to do, but it speaks something very great to say that he <hi type="italic">does nothing</hi> but what he <hi type="italic">reveals to them,</hi> as if they were <hi type="italic">the men of his counsel. Shall I hide from Abraham,</hi> who is a prophet, <hi type="italic">the thing which I do?</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.18.17">Gen. xviii. 17</reference>. God will therefore be sure to reckon with those that put contempt on the prophets, whom he puts this honour upon. 2. The prophets cannot but make that known to the people which God has made known to them (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord God has spoken; who can but prophesy?</hi> His prophets, to whom he has spoken in secret by dreams and visions, cannot but speak in public to the people what they have heard from God. They are so full of those things themselves, so well assured concerning them, and so much affected with them, that they cannot but speak of them; for <hi type="italic">out of the abundance of the heart</hi> the mouth will speak. <hi type="italic">I believed; therefore have I spoken,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.4.20">Acts iv. 20</reference>. Nay, and besides the prophetic impulse which went along with the inspiration, and made the word <hi type="italic">like a fire in their bones</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.9">Jer. xx. 9</reference>), they received a command from God to deliver what they had been charged with; and they would have been false to their trust if they had not done it. <hi type="italic">Necessity was laid upon them,</hi> as upon the preachers of the gospel, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.16">1 Cor. ix. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen20119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20120" type="x-p"/> VII. Let them know that they ought to tremble before God upon the fair warning he had given them, as they would, 1. Upon the sounding of a trumpet, to give notice of the approach of the enemy, that all may stand upon their guard and stand to their arms: <hi type="italic">Shall a trumpet be blown in the city, and the people be not afraid,</hi> or <hi type="italic">run together?</hi> so some read it, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.6">v. 6</reference>. Will they not immediately come together in a fright, to consider what is best to be done for the common safety? Yet when God by his prophets gives them notice of their danger, and summons them to come and enlist themselves under his banner, it makes no impression; they will sooner give credit to a watchman on their walls than to a prophet sent of God, will sooner obey the summons of the governor of their city than the orders given them by the Governor of the world. God says, <hi type="italic">Hearken to the voice of the trumpet;</hi> but <hi type="italic">they will not hearken,</hi> nay, and they tell him plainly that they will not, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.17">Jer. vi. 17</reference>. 2. Upon the roaring of a lion. God is sometimes <hi type="italic">as a lion, and a young lion, to the house of Judah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.5.14">Hos. v. 14</reference>. The lion roars before he tears; thus God warns before he wounds. If therefore the lion roars upon a poor traveller (as he did against Samson, <reference osisRef="Judg.14.5">Judg. xiv. 5</reference>), he cannot but be put into great consternation; yet the <hi type="italic">Lord roars out of Zion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.2">ch. i. 2</reference>), and none are afraid, but they go on securely as if they were in no danger. Note, The fair warning given to a careless world, if it be not taken, will aggravate its condemnation another day. The lion roared, and they were not moved with fear to prepare an ark. O the amazing stupidity of an unbelieving world, that will not be wrought upon, no, not by the <hi type="italic">terrors of the Lord!</hi>
entries.398125b779b3330f2ab37f1201a6433fe9bb950b: <div eID="gen20120" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Israel Convicted and Condemned. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 790.)</title> <div sID="gen20121" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Publish in the palaces at Ashdod, and in the palaces in the land of Egypt, and say, Assemble yourselves upon the mountains of Samaria, and behold the great tumults in the midst thereof, and the oppressed in the midst thereof. <hi type="super">10</hi> For they know not to do right, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , who store up violence and robbery in their palaces. <hi type="super">11</hi> Therefore thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; An adversary <hi type="italic">there shall be</hi> even round about the land; and he shall bring down thy strength from thee, and thy palaces shall be spoiled. <hi type="super">12</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; As the shepherd taketh out of the mouth of the lion two legs, or a piece of an ear; so shall the children of Israel be taken out that dwell in Samaria in the corner of a bed, and in Damascus <hi type="italic">in</hi> a couch. <hi type="super">13</hi> Hear ye, and testify in the house of Jacob, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , the God of hosts, <hi type="super">14</hi> That in the day that I shall visit the transgressions of Israel upon him I will also visit the altars of Bethel: and the horns of the altar shall be cut off, and fall to the ground. <hi type="super">15</hi> And I will smite the winter house with the summer house; and the houses of ivory shall perish, and the great houses shall have an end, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen20121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20122" type="x-p"/> The Israelites are here again convicted and condemned, and particular notice given of the crimes they are convicted of and the punishment they are condemned to. <div eID="gen20122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20123" type="x-p"/> 1. Notice is given of it to their neighbours. The prophet is ordered to <hi type="italic">publish it in the palaces of Ashdod,</hi> one of the chief cities of the Philistines; nay, the summons must go further, even to <hi type="italic">the palaces in the land of Egypt.</hi> "The great men of both those nations, that dwell in the palaces, that are inquisitive concerning the affairs of the neighboring nations, and are conversant with the public intelligence, let them <hi type="italic">assemble themselves upon the mountains of Samaria,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Amos.3.9">v. 9</reference>. There, upon <hi type="italic">a throne high and lifted up,</hi> the judgment is set. Samaria is the criminal that is to be tried; let them be present at the trial, for it shall be (as other trials are) public, in the face of the country; let them make an appointment to meet there from all parts, to judge between God and his vineyard. God appeals to all impartial righteous men, <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.45">Ezek. xxiii. 45</reference>. They will all subscribe to the equity of his proceedings when they see how the case stands. Note, God's controversies with sinners do not fear a scrutiny; even Philistines and Egyptians will be made to see, and say, that <hi type="italic">the ways of the Lord are equal,</hi> but <hi type="italic">our ways are unequal.</hi> They are likewise summoned to attend, not only that they may justify God and be witness for him that he deals fairly, but that they may themselves take warning; for, if <hi type="italic">judgment begin at the house of God,</hi> as they see it does, what shall be the end of those that are strangers to him? <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17">1 Pet. iv. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">If this be done in a green tree, what shall be done in a dry?</hi> Or this intimates that the sin of Israel had been so notorious that the neighboring nations could come in witnesses against them, and therefore it was fit that their punishment should be so. "If it could have been concealed, we would have said, <hi type="italic">Tell it not in Gath; publish it not in the streets of Ashkelon;</hi>" but why should their friends consult their reputation, when they themselves do not consult it? If they have grown impudent in sin, let them bear the shame: "<hi type="italic">Publish</hi> it in <hi type="italic">Ashdod,</hi> in <hi type="italic">Egypt.</hi>" <div eID="gen20123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20124" type="x-p"/> 1. Let them see how black the charge is, and how well proved. Let them observe the behaviour of the inhabitants of Samaria; let them look off from the adjacent hills, and they may see how rude and boisterous they are, and hear how loud they cry of their sin is, as was that of Sodom. (1.) Look into their streets and you will see nothing but riot and disorder, <hi type="italic">great tumults in the midst thereof;</hi> reason and justice are upon all occasions run down by the noise and fury of an outrageous mob, the dominion of which is the sin and shame of any people, and is likely to be their ruin. (2.) Look into their prisons, and you will see them filled with injured innocents: <hi type="italic">The oppressed are in the midst thereof,</hi> thrown down and crushed by their oppressors, overpowered and overwhelmed, and <hi type="italic">they had no comforter,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.1">Eccl. iv. 1</reference>. (3.) Look into their courts of justice, and you will see that those who preside in those courts <hi type="italic">know not to do right,</hi> because they have always been accustomed to do wrong; they act as if they had no notion at all of the thing called justice, are in no care to do justice themselves nor to see that others do justice. (4.) Look into their treasures and stores, and you will see them replenished with <hi type="italic">violence and robbery,</hi> with that which was unjustly got and is still unjustly kept. Thus <hi type="italic">they have heaped treasures together for the last days,</hi> but it will prove a <hi type="italic">treasure of wrath against the day of wrath.</hi> It may well be said, Those <hi type="italic">know not to do right</hi> who think to enrich themselves by doing wrong. <div eID="gen20124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20125" type="x-p"/> 2. Let them see how heavy the doom is, and how well executed, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.11-Amos.3.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. <div eID="gen20125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20126" type="x-p"/> (1.) Their country shall be invaded and ruined; and observe how the punishment answers to the sin. [1.] <hi type="italic">Great tumults</hi> are <hi type="italic">in the midst of the land,</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">an adversary shall be even round about the land;</hi> the Assyrian forces shall surround it and break in upon it on every side. Note, When sin is harboured and indulged in the midst of a people they can expect no other than that adversaries should be round about them, so that, go which way they will, they go into the mouth of danger, <reference osisRef="Luke.19.43">Luke xix. 43</reference>. [2.] They strengthened themselves in their wickedness, but the enemy shall <hi type="italic">bring down their strength</hi> from them, that strength which they abused in oppressing the poor, and doing violence to all about them. Note, That power which is made an instrument of unrighteousness will justly be brought down and broken. [3.] They <hi type="italic">stored up robbery in their palaces,</hi> and therefore their <hi type="italic">palaces shall be spoiled;</hi> for what is got and kept wrongfully will not be kept long. Even palaces will be no protection to fraud and oppression; but the greatest of men, if they have spoiled others, shall themselves be spoiled, for <hi type="italic">the Lord is the avenger of all such.</hi> <div eID="gen20126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20127" type="x-p"/> (2.) Their countrymen shall not escape, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.12">v. 12</reference>. They shall be in the hands of the enemy, as a lamb in the mouth of a lion, all devoured and eaten up, and they shall be utterly unable to make an resistance; and if any do make their escape, so as neither to fall by the sword or go into captivity, yet they shall be very few, and those of the meanest and least considerable, like <hi type="italic">two legs,</hi> or <hi type="italic">shanks,</hi> of a lamb, <hi type="italic">or,</hi> it may be, <hi type="italic">a piece of an ear,</hi> which the lion drops, or <hi type="italic">the shepherd</hi> takes from him, when he has eaten the whole body; so, perhaps, here and there one may escape from Samaria and from Damascus, when the king of Assyria shall fall upon them both, but none to make any account of; and those that do escape shall do so with the utmost difficult and hazard, by hiding themselves in the <hi type="italic">corner of a bed</hi> or under the <hi type="italic">bed's feet,</hi> which intimates that their spirits shall sneak shamefully in the time of danger. They shall not hide themselves in dens and caves, but in the <hi type="italic">corner of a bed,</hi> or the <hi type="italic">piece of a bed,</hi> such as poor people must be content with. They shall very narrowly escape, as it is foretold concerning the last destruction of Jerusalem that there shall be <hi type="italic">two in a bed together, one taken and the other left.</hi> Note, When God's judgments come forth against a people with commission it will be in vain to think of escaping them. Some make their <hi type="italic">dwelling in the corner of a bed,</hi> and <hi type="italic">in a couch,</hi> to denote their present security and sensuality; they are at ease, as <hi type="italic">in a bed,</hi> or <hi type="italic">on a couch,</hi> but, when God comes to contend with them, he shall make them uneasy, shall take them away out of the bed of their sloth and slumber. Those that stretch themselves lazily upon their couches when God's judgments are abroad shall <hi type="italic">go captive with the first that go captive.</hi> <div eID="gen20127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20128" type="x-p"/> II. Notice is given of it to themselves, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.13">v. 13</reference>. Let this be <hi type="italic">testified,</hi> and <hi type="italic">heard, in the house of Jacob,</hi> among all the seed of Israel, for it is spoken by <hi type="italic">the Lord God, the God of hosts,</hi> who has authority to pass this sentence and ability to execute it; let them know from him that the day is at hand when God will <hi type="italic">visit the transgressions of Israel upon him,</hi> when he will enquire into them and reckon for them: there will come <hi type="italic">a day of visitation,</hi> a day of punishment, and in that day all those things they are proud of, and put confidence in, shall fail them, and so they shall smart for the sins they have been guilty of about them. 1. Woe to <hi type="italic">their altars,</hi> for God will <hi type="italic">visit</hi> them. He will enquire into the sins they have been guilty of at their altars, and bring into the account all their superstition and idolatry, all their expenses on their false gods, and all their expectations from them; and he will lay the altars themselves under the marks of his displeasure, for <hi type="italic">the horns of the altar shall be cut off,</hi> and <hi type="italic">fall to the ground,</hi> and with them the altar itself demolished and broken to pieces. We find the altar at Bethel prophesied against (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.2">1 Kings xiii. 2</reference>), and immediately <hi type="italic">rent</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.3">v. 3</reference>), and that prophecy fulfilled with <hi type="italic">Josiah burnt men's bones upon it,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.15-2Kgs.23.16">2 Kings xxiii. 15, 16</reference>. This seconds that prophecy, and seems to point at the same event. Note, If men will not destroy idolatrous altars, God will, and those with them that had them in veneration. Some make <hi type="italic">the horns of the altar</hi> to signify all those things which they flee to for refuge, and trust in, and which they make their sanctuary: they shall all be cut off, so that they shall have nothing to take hold of. 2. Woe to their houses, for God will visit them too. He will enquire into the sins they have been guilty of in their houses, the robbery that have stored up in their houses, and the luxury in which they lived: <hi type="italic">and I will smite the winter-house with the summer-house,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.3.15">v. 15</reference>. Their nobility, and gentry, and rich merchants, had their winter-houses in the city and their summer-houses in the country, so nice were they in guarding against the inconveniences of the winter when the country was thought too cold, and of the summer when the city was thought too hot, though the climate of that good land was so temperate, like that of ours, that neither the cold nor heat was ever in extremity. They indulged a foolish affectation of change and variety; but God will, either by war or by the earthquake, smite both the winter-house and the summer-house; neither shall serve to shelter them from his judgments. <hi type="italic">The houses of ivory</hi> (so called because the ceiling, or wainscot, or some of the ornaments of them, were edged or inlaid with ivory) <hi type="italic">shall perish,</hi> shall be burnt or pulled down; <hi type="italic">and the great houses shall have an end;</hi> the most splendid and spacious houses, the houses of their great men, shall no longer be, or at least be no longer theirs. Note, The pomp or pleasantness of men's houses will be so far from fortifying them against God's judgments that it will make them the more grievous and vexatious, as their extravagance about them will be put to the score of their sins and follies.  <chapter eID="Amos.3"/> <div eID="gen20128" type="x-p"/>

entries.23e2a9a87ea1a9cefd2f7e8777d61b898aff1525: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12537"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Amos.3.1-Amos.3.15">Am 3:1-15</reference>. God's Extraordinary Love, Being Repaid by Israel with Ingratitude, of Necessity Calls for Judgments, Which the Prophets Announce, Not at Random, but by God's Commission, Which They Cannot but Fulfil. The Oppression Prevalent in Israel Will Bring Down Ruin on All Save a Small Remnant.</title> <div sID="gen23074" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12537"/><hi type="bold">1. children of Israel--</hi>not merely the ten tribes, but "the whole family brought up from Egypt"; all the descendants of Jacob, including Judah and Benjamin. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.8.3">Jr 8:3</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Mic.2.3">Mi 2:3</reference>, on "family" for the nation. However, as the prophecy following refers to the ten tribes, they must be chiefly, if not solely, meant: they were the majority of the nation; and so Amos concedes what they so often boasted, that they were the elect people of God [Calvin], but implies that this only heightens their sins. <div eID="gen23074" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc7d37a7ee242e89dda271c2bb8e26dcbea6c144: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12538"/><div sID="gen23075" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12538"/><hi type="bold">2. You only have I known--</hi>that is, acknowledged as My people, and treated with peculiar favor (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.5">Ex 19:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.4.20">De 4:20</reference>). Compare the use of "know," <reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Psa 1:6</reference>; 144:3; <reference osisRef="John.10.14">Joh 10:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">2Ti 2:19</reference>.<div eID="gen23075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23076" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">therefore I will punish--</hi>the greater the privileges, the heavier the punishment for the abuse of them; for to the other offenses there is added, in this case, ingratitude. When God's people do not glorify Him, He glorifies Himself by punishing them. <div eID="gen23076" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd7640d01bbf4fa12d3e680ef227d386c4008c0e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12539"/><div sID="gen23077" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12539"/>3-6. Here follow several questions of a parable-like kind, to awaken conviction in the people.<div eID="gen23077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23078" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Can two walk together, except they be agreed?--</hi>Can God's prophets be so unanimous in prophesying against you, if God's Spirit were not joined with them, or if their prophecies were false? The Israelites were "at ease," not believing that God was with the prophets in their denunciations of coming ruin to the nation (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Am 6:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.3">3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.18">1Ki 22:18</reference>, 24, 27; <reference osisRef="Jer.43.2">Jr 43:2</reference>). This accords with <reference osisRef="Amos.3.7">Am 3:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.8">8</reference>. So "I will be with thy mouth" (<reference osisRef="Exod.4.12">Ex 4:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.1.8">Jr 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.10.20">Mt 10:20</reference>). If the prophets and God were not agreed, the former could not predict the future as they do. In <reference osisRef="Amos.2.12">Am 2:12</reference> He had said, the Israelites forbade the prophets prophesying; therefore, in <reference osisRef="Amos.3.3">Am 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.8">8</reference>, He asserts the agreement between the prophets and God who spake by them against Israel [Rosenmuller]. Rather, "I once walked with you" (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.12">Le 26:12</reference>) as a Father and Husband (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.5">Is 54:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.14">Jr 3:14</reference>); but now your way and Mine are utterly diverse; there can therefore be no fellowship between us such as there was (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.2">Am 3:2</reference>); I will walk with you only to "punish you"; as a "lion" walks with his "prey" (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.4">Am 3:4</reference>), as a bird-catcher with a bird [Tarnovius]. The prophets, and all servants of God, can have no fellowship with the ungodly (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.63">Psa 119:63</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.16">2Co 6:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.11">Ep 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.4">Jas 4:4</reference>). <div eID="gen23078" type="x-p"/>
entries.75d8397d9472d3ca4d96211dc0fc4bd1accbdf8b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12543"/><div sID="gen23086" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12543"/><hi type="bold">7. his secret--</hi>namely, His purpose hidden from all, until it is revealed to His prophets (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.18.17">Ge 18:17</reference>). In a wider sense, God's will is revealed to all who love God, which it is not to the world (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.14">Psa 25:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.15.15">Joh 15:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.25">17:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.26">26</reference>).<div eID="gen23086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23087" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto his servants--</hi>who being servants cannot but obey their Lord in setting forth His purpose (namely, that of judgment against Israel) (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.9">Jr 20:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.11">Eze 9:11</reference>). Therefore the fault which the ungodly find with them is groundless (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.17">1Ki 18:17</reference>). It aggravates Israel's sin, that God is not about to inflict judgment, without having fully warned the people, if haply they might repent. <div eID="gen23087" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c4c3a1552201260d49d489472ce35034133a90c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12544"/><div sID="gen23088" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12544"/>8. As when "the lion roars" (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.1.2">Am 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.3.4">Am 3:4</reference>), none can help but "fear," so when Jehovah communicates His awful message, the prophet cannot but prophesy. Find not fault with me for prophesying; I must obey God. In a wider sense true of all believers (<reference osisRef="Acts.4.20">Ac 4:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.5.29">5:29</reference>). <div eID="gen23088" type="x-p"/>
entries.4998c2004629c1d7683e64099ea620470ca03e8c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12545"/><div sID="gen23089" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12545"/><hi type="bold">9. Publish in ... palaces--</hi>as being places of greatest resort (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.10.27">Mt 10:27</reference>); and also as it is the sin of princes that he arraigns, he calls on princes (the occupants of the "palaces") to be the witnesses.<div eID="gen23089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23090" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ashdod--</hi>put for all Philistia. Convene the Philistine and the Egyptian magnates, from whom I have on various occasions rescued Israel. (The opposite formula to "Tell it not in Gath," namely, lest the heathen should glory over Israel). Even these idolaters, in looking on your enormities, will condemn you; how much more will the holy God?<div eID="gen23090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23091" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon the mountains of Samaria--</hi>on the hills surrounding and commanding the view of Samaria, the metropolis of the ten tribes, which was on a lower hill (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.1">Am 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.24">1Ki 16:24</reference>). The mountains are to be the tribunal on which the Philistines and Egyptians are to sit aloft to have a view of your crimes, so as to testify to the justice of your punishment (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.13">Am 3:13</reference>).<div eID="gen23091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23092" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tumults--</hi>caused by the violence of the princes of Israel in "oppressions" of the poor (<reference osisRef="Job.35.9">Job 35:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.1">Ec 4:1</reference>). <div eID="gen23092" type="x-p"/>
entries.67cdd690df9a5520546b2a6fb204e6a3b90d58e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12546"/><div sID="gen23093" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12546"/><hi type="bold">10. know not to do--</hi>Their moral corruption blinds their power of discernment so that they cannot do right (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.22">Jr 4:22</reference>). Not simple intellectual ignorance; the defect lay in the heart and will.<div eID="gen23093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23094" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">store up violence and robbery--</hi>that is, treasures obtained by "violence and robbery" (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.2">Pr 10:2</reference>). <div eID="gen23094" type="x-p"/>
entries.df0e50bf32a47436b465289c9bb150b52171820f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12547"/><div sID="gen23095" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12547"/>11. Translate, "An adversary (the abruptness produces a startling effect)! and that too, from every side of the land." So in the fulfilment, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.5">2Ki 17:5</reference>: "The king of Assyria (Shalmaneser) came up throughout all the land, and went up to Samaria, and besieged it three years."<div eID="gen23095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23096" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring down thy strength from thee--</hi>that is, bring thee down from thy strength (the strength on which thou didst boast thyself): all thy resources (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.15">Pr 10:15</reference>).<div eID="gen23096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23097" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">palaces shall be spoiled--</hi>a just retribution in kind (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.10">Am 3:10</reference>). The palaces in which spoils of robbery were stored up, "shall be spoiled." <div eID="gen23097" type="x-p"/>
entries.969b686c710a763d868a4f2977100fc868acc778: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12548"/><div sID="gen23098" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12548"/><hi type="bold">12. shepherd--</hi>a pastoral image, appropriately used by Amos, a shepherd himself.<div eID="gen23098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23099" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">piece of ... ear--</hi>brought by the shepherd to the owner of the sheep, so as not to have to pay for the loss (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.39">Ge 31:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.22.13">Ex 22:13</reference>). So if aught of Israel escapes, it shall be a miracle of God's goodness. It shall be but a scanty remnant. There is a kind of goat in the East the ears of which are a foot long, and proportionally broad. Perhaps the reference is to this. Compare on the image <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.34">1Sa 17:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.35">35</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.17">2Ti 4:17</reference>.<div eID="gen23099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23100" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that dwell in Samaria in the corner of a bed--</hi>that is, that live luxuriously in Samaria (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Am 6:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.4">4</reference>). "A bed" means here the Oriental divan, a raised part of the room covered with cushions.<div eID="gen23100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23101" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Damascus in a couch--</hi>Jeroboam II had lately restored Damascus to Israel (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.25">2Ki 14:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.28">28</reference>). So the Israelites are represented as not merely in "the corner of a bed," as in Samaria, but "in a (whole) couch," at Damascus, living in luxurious ease. Of these, now so luxurious, soon but a remnant shall be left by the foe. The destruction of Damascus and that of Samaria shall be conjoined; as here their luxurious lives, and subsequently under Pekah and Rezin their inroads on Judah, were combined (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.1-Isa.8.8">Is 7:1-8; 8</reference>:4, 9; 17:3). The parallelism of "Samaria" to "Damascus," and the Septuagint favor English Version rather than Gesenius: "on a damask couch." The Hebrew pointing, though generally expressing damask, may express the city "Damascus"; and many manuscripts point it so. Compare for Israel's overthrow, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.5">2Ki 17:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.9-2Kgs.18.12">18:9-12</reference>. <div eID="gen23101" type="x-p"/>
entries.8eeb293b43f8449f7c16bbd5f70920fa2514725e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12549"/><div sID="gen23102" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12549"/><hi type="bold">13. testify in the house, &c.--</hi>that is, against the house of Jacob. God calls on the same persons as in <reference osisRef="Amos.3.9">Am 3:9</reference>, namely, the heathen Philistines and the Egyptians to witness with their own eyes Samaria's corruptions above described, so that none may be able to deny the justice of Samaria's punishment [Maurer].<div eID="gen23102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23103" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God of hosts--</hi>having all the powers of heaven and earth at His command, and therefore One calculated to strike terror into the hearts of the guilty whom He threatens. <div eID="gen23103" type="x-p"/>
entries.4d7f22cee160ef0f15d4e1fe26e2f42a927d337b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12550"/><div sID="gen23104" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12550"/><hi type="bold">14. That--</hi>rather, "since," or "for." This verse is not, as English Version translates, the thing which the witnesses cited are to "testify" (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.13">Am 3:13</reference>), but the reason why God calls on the heathen to witness Samaria's guilt; namely, in order to justify the punishment which He declares He will inflict.<div eID="gen23104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23105" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will also visit ... Beth-el--</hi>the golden calves which were the source of all "the transgressions of Israel" (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.32">1Ki 12:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.2">13:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.15">2Ki 23:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.16">16</reference>), though Israel thought that by them their transgressions were atoned for and God's favor secured.<div eID="gen23105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23106" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">horns of the altar--</hi>which used to be sprinkled with the blood of victims. They were horn-like projecting points at the corners of ancient altars. The singular, "altar," refers to the great altar erected by Jeroboam to the calves. The "altars," plural, refer to the lesser ones made in imitation of the great one (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.5">2Ch 34:5</reference>, compare with <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.2">1Ki 13:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.8.11">Ho 8:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.10.1">10:1</reference>). <div eID="gen23106" type="x-p"/>
entries.46b9519b8b5ee93ae99044368a44dff5d7532f45: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12551"/><div sID="gen23107" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12551"/><hi type="bold">15. winter ... summer house--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Judg.3.20">Jud 3:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.36.22">Jr 36:22</reference>). Winter houses of the great were in sheltered positions facing the south to get all possible sunshine, summer houses in forests and on hills, facing the east and north.<div eID="gen23107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23108" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">houses of ivory--</hi>having their walls, doors, and ceilings inlaid with ivory. So Ahab's house (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.39">1Ki 22:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.45.8">Psa 45:8</reference>). <chapter eID="Amos.3"/>

entries.35a3ccd14d634f681a439101c00e6ac271a8dc52: <div eID="gen34283" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen34284" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34285" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34285" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34284" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34286" type="x-p"/> This chapter begins with reproving the twelve tribes in general, <reference osisRef="Amo.3.1">Amo 3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amo.3.2">Amo 3:2</reference>; and then particularly the kingdom of Israel, whose capital was Samaria. Thee prophet assures them that, while they were at variance with God, it would be unreasonable in them to expect his presence or favor, <reference osisRef="Amo.3.3-Amo.3.8">Amo 3:3-8</reference>. Other neighboring nations are then called upon to take warning from the judgments about to be inflicted upon the house of Israel, which would be so general that only a small remnant should escape them, <reference osisRef="Amo.3.9-Amo.3.15">Amo 3:9-15</reference>. The image used by the prophet on this occasion, (see <reference osisRef="Amo.3.12">Amo 3:12</reference>), and borrowed from his former calling, is very natural and significant, and not a little dignified by the inspired writer's lofty air and manner. <div eID="gen34286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34287" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen34287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34288" type="x-p"/> Against the whole family - That is, all, both the kingdoms of Israel and Judah. In this all the twelve tribes are included.
entries.c86ef090af6194f08dafe1a18cd9525e95d618a4: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen34288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34289" type="x-p"/> You only have I known - I have taken no other people to be my own people. I have approved of you, loved you, fed, sustained, and defended you; but because you have forsaken me, have become idolatrous and polluted, therefore will I punish you. And the punishment shall be in proportion to the privileges you have enjoyed, and the grace you have abused.
entries.d04cde6d3441b02cb1320aa8dc79c695aabcf473: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen34289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34290" type="x-p"/> Can two walk together - While ye loved and served me, I dwelt in you and walked among you. Now ye are become alienated from me, your nature and mine are totally opposite. I am holy, ye are unholy. We are no longer agreed, and can no longer walk together. I can no longer hold communion with you. I must cast you out. The similes in this and the three following verses are all chosen to express the same thing, viz., that no calamities or judgments can fall upon any people but by the express will of God, on account of their iniquities; and that whatever his prophets have foretold, they have done it by direct revelation from their Maker; and that God has the highest and most cogent reason for inflicting the threatened calamities. This correctness of the prophets' predictions shows that they and I are in communion.
entries.8df83ea360318a654ffacbd3a048f3331b989e7c: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen34290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34291" type="x-p"/> Will a lion roar - Should I threaten such a judgment without cause?
entries.0b8223773e2c1c7ce1a8508a65bce0064339aea7: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen34291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34292" type="x-p"/> Can a bird fall in a snare - Can ye, as a sinful people, fall into calamities which I have not appointed? <div eID="gen34292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34293" type="x-p"/> Shall one take up a snare - and have taken nothing - Will the snare be removed before it has caught the expected prey? - shall I remove my judgments till they are fully accomplished? This is a curious passage, and deserves farther consideration. The original, literally translated, is nearly as follows: "Shall the trap arise from the ground; and catching, shall it not catch?" Here is a plain allusion to such traps as we employ to catch rats, foxes, etc. The jaws of the trap opening backward, press strongly upon a spring so as to keep it down; and a key passing over one jaw, and hooking on a table in the center, the trap continues with expanded jaws, till any thing touch the table, when the key, by the motion of the table, being loosened, the spring recovers all its elastic power, and throws up the jaws of the trap, and their serrated edges either close in each other, or on the prey that has moved the table of the trap. Will then the jaws of such a trap suddenly spring up from the ground, on which before they were lying flat, and catch nothing? Shall they let the prey that was within them escape? Certainly not. So my trap is laid for these offenders; and when it springs up, (and they themselves will soon by their transgressions free the key), shall not the whole family of Israel be inclosed in it? Most certainly they shall. This is a singular and very remarkable passage, and, when properly understood, is beautifully expressive.
entries.3efc153b624b6550ff2070ccb575f3196ff6fbff: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen34293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34294" type="x-p"/> Shall a trumpet be blown - The sign of alarm and invasion. <div eID="gen34294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34295" type="x-p"/> And the people not be afraid? - Not take the alarm, and provide for their defense and safety? <div eID="gen34295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34296" type="x-p"/> Shall there be evil in a city - Shall there be any public calamity on the wicked, that is not an effect of my displeasure? The word does not mean moral evil, but punishment for sin; calamities falling on the workers of iniquity. Natural evil is the punishment of moral evil: God sends the former when the latter is persisted in.
entries.2cc417a52bf42264f9241eae3c5a6421692dccb9: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen34296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34297" type="x-p"/> Surely the Lord God will do nothing - In reference to the punishment, correction, or blessing of his people: - <div eID="gen34297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34298" type="x-p"/> But he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets - They are in strict correspondence with him, and he shows them things to come. Such secrets of God are revealed to them, that they may inform the people; that, by repentance and conversion, they may avoid the evil, and, by walking closely with God, secure the continuance of his favor.
entries.57c6f1e4cbc0c9f609810e36f06390ff961f8cc8: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen34298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34299" type="x-p"/> The lion hath roared - God hath sent forth a terrible alarm, Who will not fear? Can any hear such denunciations of Divine wrath and not tremble? <div eID="gen34299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34300" type="x-p"/> The Lord God hath spoken - And those only who are in communion with him have heard the speech. Who can but prophesy? Who can help proclaiming at large the judgment threatened against the nation? <div eID="gen34300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34301" type="x-p"/> But I think נבא naba, here, is to be taken in its natural and ideal signification, to pray, supplicate, or deprecate vengeance. The Lord hath spoken of punishment - who can help supplicating his mercy, that his judgments may be averted?
entries.5082bf49b1eb5dd0341ae1bbf6cab89008718cee: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen34301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34302" type="x-p"/> Publish in the palaces - The housetops or flat roofs were the places from which public declarations were made. See on <reference osisRef="Isa.21.1">Isa 21:1</reference> (note), and on <reference osisRef="Mat.10.27">Mat 10:27</reference> (note). See whether in those places there be not tumults, oppressions, and rapine sufficient to excite my wrath against them.
entries.1459fa2ba2485a914ab07ab3aa40bd56a27b5fbd: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen34302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34303" type="x-p"/> For they know not to do right - So we may naturally say that they who are doing wrong, and to their own prejudice and ruin, must certainly be ignorant of what is right, and what is their own interest. But we say again "There are none so blind as those who will not see." Their eyes, saith the Lord, they have closed.
entries.6885f97c0bcf05f74467fafdf3d1e9bfc403871b: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen34303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34304" type="x-p"/> An adversary, round about the land - Ye shall not be able to escape, wherever ye turn, ye shall meet a foe.
entries.34d7901c5c6dbbfbe7dd9b4ee8590fd68af60469: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen34304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34305" type="x-p"/> As the shepherd taketh out of the mouth of the lion - Scarcely any of you shall escape; and those that do shall do so with extreme difficulty, just as a shepherd, of a whole sheep carried away by a lion, can recover no more than two of its legs, or a piece of its ear, just enough to prove by the marks on those parts, that they belonged to a sheep which was his own. <div eID="gen34305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34306" type="x-p"/> So shall the children of Israel be taken out - Those of them that escape these judgments shall escape with as great difficulty, and be of as little worth, as the two legs and piece of an ear that shall be snatched out of the lion's mouth. We know that when the Babylonians carried away the people into Chaldea they left behind only a few, and those the refuse of the land. <div eID="gen34306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34307" type="x-p"/> In the corner of a bed - As the corner is the most honorable place in the East, and a couch in the corner of a room is the place of the greatest distinction; so the words in the text may mean, that even the metropolitan cities, which are in the corner - in the most honorable place - of the land, whether Samaria in Israel, or Damascus in Syria, shall not escape these judgments; and if any of the distinguished persons who dwell in them escape, it must be with as great difficulty as the fragments above-mentioned have been recovered from a lion. The passage is obscure. Mr. Harmer has taken great pains to illustrate it; but I fear with but little success. A general sense is all we can arrive at.
entries.788d1fe5e72ec97877289b57c09277c0b2d178f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen34307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34308" type="x-p"/> Hear ye - This is an address to the prophet.
entries.8ed644b545780f3c8530740e04bfa87d81f2fd2f: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen34308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34309" type="x-p"/> In the day that I shall visit - When Josiah made a reformation in the land he destroyed idolatry, pulled down the temples and altars that had been consecrated to idol worship, and even burnt the bones of the priests of Baal and the golden calves upon their own altars. See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.15">2Kgs 23:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.16">2Kgs 23:16</reference>, etc.
entries.7e0b6cf81e1607eee27d2cb28205a4cbc92078f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen34309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34310" type="x-p"/> I will smite the winter house with the summer house - I will not only destroy the poor habitations and villages in the country, but I will destroy those of the nobility and gentry as well as the lofty palaces in the fortified cities in which they dwell in the winter season, as those light and elegant seats in which they spend the summer season. Dr. Shaw observes that "the hills and valleys round about Algiers are all over beautified with gardens and country seats, whither the inhabitants of better fashion retire during the heats of the summer season. They are little white houses, shaded with a variety of fruit trees and evergreens, which beside shade and retirement, afford a gay and delightful prospect toward the sea. The gardens are all well stocked with melons, fruits, and pot herbs of all kinds; and (which is chiefly regarded in these hot countries) each of them enjoys a great command of water." <div eID="gen34310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34311" type="x-p"/> And the houses of ivory - Those remarkable for their magnificence and their ornaments, not built of ivory, but in which ivory vessels, ornaments, and inlaying abounded. Thus, then, the winter houses and the summer houses, the great houses and the houses of uncommon splendor, shall all perish. There should be a total desolation in the land. No kind of house should be a refuge, and no kind of habitation should be spared. Ahab had at Samaria a house that was called the ivory house, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.39">1Kgs 22:39</reference>. This may be particularly referred to in this place. We cannot suppose that a house constructed entirely of ivory can be intended.  <chapter eID="Amos.3"/> <div eID="gen34311" type="x-p"/>

entries.d09f6df41d0a5cfd4bd7401e774c94733411bb6c: <div eID="gen16364" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">II. Prophecies Concerning Israel - <reference osisRef="Amos.3.6">Amos 3-6</reference></title> <div sID="gen16365" type="x-p"/> Although the expression “Hear this word,” which is repeated at the commencement of <reference osisRef="Amos.3.1-Amos.3.15">Amo 3:1-15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.4.1-Amos.4.13">Amo 4:1-13</reference> and 5, suggests the idea of three addresses, the contents of these chapters show that they do not contain three separate addresses delivered to the people by Amos at different times, but that they group together the leading thoughts of appeals delivered by word of mouth, so as to form one long admonition to repentance. Commencing with the proofs of his right to predict judgment to the nation on account of its sins (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.1-Amos.3.8">Amo 3:1-8</reference>), the prophet exposes the wickedness of Israel in general (ch. 3:9-4:3), and then shows the worthlessness of the nation’s trust in idolatry (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.4-Amos.4.13">Amo 4:4-13</reference>), and lastly announces the destruction of the kingdom as the inevitable consequence of the prevailing injustice and ungodliness (ch. 5 and <reference osisRef="Amos.6.1-Amos.6.14">Amo 6:1-14</reference>). <div eID="gen16365" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Announcement of the Judgment - Hos 3:1-5</title> <div sID="gen16366" type="x-p"/> Because the Lord has chosen Israel to be His people, He must visit all its sins (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.2">Amo 3:2</reference>), and has commissioned the prophet to announce this punishment (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.3-Amos.3.8">Amo 3:3-8</reference>). As Israel has heaped up oppression, violence, and wickedness, an enemy will come upon the land and plunder Samaria, and cause its inhabitants to perish, and demolish the altars of Bethel, and destroy the capital (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.9-Amos.3.15">Amo 3:9-15</reference>). <div eID="gen16366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16367" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Amos.3.1-Amos.3.2">Amo 3:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen16367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16368" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Amos.3.1">Amo 3:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Amos.3.2">Amo 3:2</reference> contain the introduction and the leading thought of the whole of the prophetic proclamation. Amo 3:1. <hi type="italic">“Hear this word which Jehovah speaketh concerning you, O sons of Israel, concerning the whole family which I have brought up out of the land of Egypt, saying:</hi> Amo 3:2. <hi type="italic">You only have I acknowledge of all the families of the earth; therefore will I visit all your iniquities upon you.” </hi> The word of the Lord is addressed to all the family of Israel, which God had brought up out of Egypt, that is to say, to all the twelve tribes of the covenant nation, although in what follows it is the ten tribes of Israel alone who are primarily threatened with the destruction of the kingdom, to indicate at the very outset that Judah might anticipate a similar fate if it did not turn to its God with sincerity. The threat is introduced by the thought that its divine election would not secure the sinful nation against punishment, but that, on the contrary, the relation of grace into which the Lord had entered with Israel demanded the punishment of all evil deeds. This cuts off the root of all false confidence in divine election. “To whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required. The greater the measure of grace, the greater also is the punishment if it is neglected or despised.” This is the fundamental law of the kingdom of God. ידע does not mean to know, to become acquainted with, or to take knowledge of a person (Hitzig), but acknowledge. Acknowledgment on the part of God is not merely taking notice, but is energetic, embracing man in his inmost being, embracing and penetrating with divine love; so that ידע not only includes the idea of love and care, as in Hos 13:5, but expresses generally the gracious fellowship of the Lord with Israel, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.18.19">Gen 18:19</reference>, and is practically equivalent to electing, including both the motive and the result of election. And because Jehovah had acknowledged, i.e., had singled out and chosen Israel as the nation best fitted to be the vehicle of His salvation, He must of necessity punish all its misdeeds, in order to purify it from the dross of sin, and make it a holy vessel of His saving grace.
entries.23cb1c0ecabcc070f3e6ef54818c45a716365f23: <reference osisRef="Amos.3.3-Amos.3.8">Amo 3:3-8</reference> <div eID="gen16368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16369" type="x-p"/> But this truth met with contradiction in the nation itself. The proud self-secure sinners would not hear such prophesying as this (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.2.4">Amo 2:4</reference>; Amo 7:10.). Amos therefore endeavours, before making any further announcement of the judgment of God, to establish his right and duty to prophesy, by a chain-like series of similes drawn from life. V. 3. <hi type="italic">“Do two walk together without having agreed?</hi> Amo 3:4. <hi type="italic">Does the lion roar in the forest, and he has no prey? does the young lion utter his cry out of his den, without having taken anything?</hi> Amo 3:5. <hi type="italic">Does the bird fall into the trap on the ground, when there is no snare for him? does the trap rise up from the earth without making a capture?</hi> Amo 3:6. <hi type="italic">Or is the trumpet blown in the city, and the people are not alarmed? or does misfortune happen in the city, and Jehovah has not done it?</hi> Amo 3:7. <hi type="italic">For the Lord Jehovah does nothing at all, without having revealed His secret to His servants the prophets.</hi> Amo 3:8. <hi type="italic">The lion has roared; who does not fear? the Lord Jehovah hath spoken; who must not prophesy?” </hi> The contents of these verses are not to be reduced to the general thought, that a prophet could no more speak without a divine impulse than any other effect could take place without a cause. There was certainly no need for a long series of examples, such as we have in <reference osisRef="Amos.3.3-Amos.3.6">Amo 3:3-6</reference>, to substantiate or illustrate the thought, which a reflecting hearer would hardly have disputed, that there was a connection between cause and effect. The examples are evidently selected with the view of showing that the utterances of the prophet originate with God. This is obvious enough in <reference osisRef="Amos.3.7">Amo 3:7</reference>, Amo 3:8. The first clause, “Do two men walk together, without having agreed as to their meeting?” (<hi type="italic">nō‛Ad</hi>, to betake one’s self to a place, to meet together at an appointed place or an appointed time; compare <reference osisRef="Job.2.11">Job 2:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.11.5">Jos 11:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.6.2">Neh 6:2</reference>; not merely to agree together), contains something more than the trivial truth, that two persons do not take a walk together without a previous arrangement. The two who walk together are Jehovah and the prophet (Cyril); not Jehovah and the nation, to which the judgment is predicted (Cocceius, Marck, and others). Amos went as prophet to Samaria or Bethel, because the Lord had sent him thither to preach judgment to the sinful kingdom. But God would not threaten judgment if He had not a nation ripe for judgment before Him. The lion which roars when it has the prey before it is Jehovah (cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.1.2">Amo 1:2</reference>; Hos 11:10, etc.). טרף אין לו is not to be interpreted according to the second clause, as signifying “without having got possession of its prey” (Hitzig), for the lion is accustomed to roar when it has the prey before it and there is no possibility of its escape, and before it actually seizes it (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.5.29">Isa 5:29</reference>).<note placement="foot">The most terrible feature in the roaring of a lion is that with this <hi type="italic">clarigatio</hi>, or, if you prefer it, with this <hi type="italic">classicum</hi>, it declares war. And after the roar there immediately follows both slaughter and laceration. For, as a rule, it only roars with that sharp roar when it has the prey in sight, upon which it immediately springs (Bochart, <hi type="italic">Hieroz.</hi> ii. 25ff., ed. Ros.).</note> <div eID="gen16369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16370" type="x-p"/> On the contrary, the perfect <hi type="italic">lâkjad</hi> in the second clause is to be interpreted according to the first clause, not as relating to the roar of satisfaction with which the lion devours the prey in its den (Baur), but as a perfect used to describe a thing which was as certain as if it had already occurred. A lion has made a capture not merely when it has actually seized the prey and torn it in pieces, but when the prey has approached so near that it cannot possibly escape. <hi type="italic">Kephı̄r</hi> is the young lion which already goes in pursuit of prey, and is to be distinguished from the young of the lion, <hi type="italic">gūr</hi> (<hi type="italic">catulus leonis</hi>), which cannot yet go in search of prey (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.19.2-Ezek.19.3">Eze 19:2-3</reference>). The two similes have the same meaning. The second strengthens the first by the assertion that God not only has before Him the nation that is ripe for judgment, but that He has it in His power. <div eID="gen16370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16371" type="x-p"/> The similes in <reference osisRef="Amos.3.5">Amo 3:5</reference> do not affirm the same as those in <reference osisRef="Amos.3.4">Amo 3:4</reference>, but contain the new thought, that Israel has deserved the destruction which threatens it. <hi type="italic">Pach</hi>, a snare, and <hi type="italic">mōqēsh</hi>, a trap, are frequently used synonymously; but here they are distinguished, <hi type="italic">pach</hi> denoting a bird-net, and <hi type="italic">mōqēsh</hi> a springe, a snare which holds the bird fast. The earlier translators have taken <hi type="italic">mōqēsh</hi> in the sense of <hi type="italic">yōqēsh</hi>, and understand it as referring to the bird-catcher; and Baur proposes to alter the text accordingly. But there is no necessity for this; and it is evidently unsuitable, since it is not requisite for a bird-catcher to be at hand, in order that the bird should be taken in a snare. The suffix <hi type="italic">lâh</hi> refers to <hi type="italic">tsippōr</hi>, and the thought is this: in order to catch a bird in the net, a springe (gin) must be laid for it. So far as the fact itself is concerned, <hi type="italic">mōqēsh</hi> is “evidently that which is necessarily followed by falling into the net; and in this instance it is sinfulness” (Hitzig); so that the meaning of the figure would be this: “Can destruction possibly overtake you, unless your sin draws you into it?” (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.2.35">Jer 2:35</reference>). In the second clause <hi type="italic">pach</hi> is the subject, and ועלה is used for the ascent or springing up of the net. Hitzig has given the meaning of the words correctly: “As the net does not spring up without catching the bird, that has sent it up by flying upon it, can ye imagine that when the destruction passes by, ye will not be seized by it, but will escape without injury?” (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.28.15">Isa 28:15</reference>). Jehovah, however, causes the evil to be foretold. As the trumpet, when blown in the city, frightens the people out of their self-security, so will the voice of the prophet, who proclaims the coming evil, excite a salutary alarm in the nation (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.1-Ezek.33.5">Eze 33:1-5</reference>). For the calamity which is bursting upon the city comes from Jehovah, is sent by Him as a punishment. This thought is explained in <reference osisRef="Amos.3.7">Amo 3:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.8">Amo 3:8</reference>, and with this explanation the whole series of figurative sentences is made perfectly clear. The approaching evil, which comes from the Lord, is predicted by the prophet, because Jehovah does not carry out His purpose without having (כּי אם, for when, except when he has, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.32.27">Gen 32:27</reference>) first of all revealed it to the prophets, that they may warn the people to repent and to reform. <hi type="italic">Sōd</hi> receives a more precise definition from the first clause of the verse, or a limitation to the purposes which God is about to fulfil upon His people. And since (this is the connection of <reference osisRef="Amos.3.8">Amo 3:8</reference>) the judgment with which the Lord is drawing near fills every one with fear, and Jehovah has spoken, i.e., has made known His counsel to the prophets, they cannot but prophesy.
entries.456c8bc62bde52377f6efe93e3ce112a52b7c46c: <reference osisRef="Amos.3.9-Amos.3.10">Amo 3:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen16371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16372" type="x-p"/> Amos has thus vindicated his own calling, and the right of all the prophets, to announce to the people the judgments of God; and now (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.9-Amos.3.15">Amo 3:9-15</reference>) he is able to proclaim without reserve what the Lord has resolved to do upon sinful Israel. Amo 3:9. <hi type="italic">“Make it heard over the palaces in Ashdod, and over the palaces in the land of Egypt, and say, Assemble yourselves upon the mountains of Samaria, and behold the great tumult in the midst thereof, and the oppressed in the heart thereof.</hi> Amo 3:10. <hi type="italic">And they know not to do the right, is the saying of Jehovah, who heap up violence and devastation in their palaces.” </hi> The speaker is Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.10">Amo 3:10</reference>), and the prophets are addressed. Jehovah summons them to send out the cry over the palaces in Ashdod and Egypt (על as in Hos 8:1), and to call the inhabitants of these palaces to hear, (1) that they may see the acts of violence, and the abominations in the palaces of Samaria; and (2) that they may be able to bear witness against Israel (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.13">Amo 3:13</reference>). This turn in the prophecy brings out to view the overflowing excess of the sins and abominations of Israel. The call of the prophets, however, is not to be uttered upon the palaces, so as to be heard far and wide (Baur and others), but over the palaces, to cause the inhabitants of them to draw near. It is they alone, and not the whole population of Ashdod and Egypt, who are to be called nigh; because only the inhabitants of the palace could pronounce a correct sentence as to the mode of life commonly adopted in the palaces of Samaria. Ashdod, one of the Philistian capitals, is mentioned by way of example, as a chief city of the uncircumcised, who were regarded by Israel as godless heathen; and Egypt is mentioned along with it, as the nation whose unrighteousness and ungodliness had once been experienced by Israel to satiety. If therefore such heathen as these are called to behold the unrighteous and dissolute conduct to be seen in the palaces, it must have been great indeed. The mountains of Samaria are not the mountains of the kingdom of Samaria, or the mountains upon which the city of Samaria was situated - for Samaria was not built upon a plurality of mountains, but upon one only (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.1">Amo 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Amo 6:1</reference>) - but the mountains round about Samaria, from which you could look into the city, built upon one isolated hill. The city, built upon the hill of <hi type="italic">Semer</hi>, was situated in a mountain caldron or basin, about two yours in diameter, which was surrounded on all sides by lofty mountains (see at 1Ki 16:24).<note placement="foot">“As the mountains round the hill of <hi type="italic">Semer</hi> are loftier than this hill itself, the enemy might easily discover the internal state of besieged Samaria.” V. de Velde, <hi type="italic">R.</hi> i. p. 282.</note><hi type="italic">Mehūmâh</hi>, noise, tumult, denotes a state of confusion, in which everything is topsy-turvy, and all justice and order are overthrown by open violence (Maurer, Baur). <hi type="italic">‛Ashūqı̄m</hi>, either the oppressed, or, taken as an abstract, the oppression of the poor (cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.2.6">Amo 2:6</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Amos.3.10">Amo 3:10</reference> the description is continued in the finite verb: they do not know how to do right; that is to say, injustice has become their nature; and they who heap up sins and violence in their palaces like treasures.
entries.452ddf520104b95ef9025e540e90ae34b6b68a4b: <reference osisRef="Amos.3.11-Amos.3.12">Amo 3:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen16372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16373" type="x-p"/> Thus do they bring about the ruin of the kingdom. Amo 3:11. <hi type="italic">“Therefore thus saith the Lord Jehovah, An enemy, and that round about the land; and he will hurl down thy glory from thee, and thy palaces are plundered.</hi> Amo 3:12. <hi type="italic">Thus saith Jehovah, As the shepherd delivers out of the mouth of the lion two shin-bones or an ear-lappet, so will the sons of Israel deliver themselves; they who sit on the corner of the couch and on the damask of the bed.” </hi> The threat is introduced in the form of an aposiopesis. צר, enemy, וּסביב הארץ, and indeed round about the land (  ו explic. as in <reference osisRef="Amos.4.10">Amo 4:10</reference>, etc.; and סביב in the construct state construed as a preposition), i.e., will come, attack the land on all sides, and take possession of it. Others regard צר as an abstract: oppression (from the Chaldee); but in this case we should have to supply <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> as the subject to והוריד; and although this is probable, it is by no means natural, as Jehovah is speaking. There is no foundation, on the other hand, for the remark, that if <hi type="italic">tsar</hi> signified the enemy, we should either find the plural צרים, or הצּר with the article (Baumgarten). The very indefiniteness of <hi type="italic">tsar</hi> suits the sententious brevity of the clause. This enemy will hurl down the splendour of Samaria, “which ornaments the top of the mountain like a crown, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.1">Isa 28:1</reference>-3” (Hitzig: עז, might, with the subordinate idea of glory), and plunder the palaces in which violence, i.e., property unrighteously acquired, is heaped up (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.10">Amo 3:10</reference>). The words are addressed to the city of Samaria, to which the feminine suffixes refer. On the fall of Samaria, and the plundering thereof, the luxurious grandees, who rest upon costly pillows, will only be able to save their life to the very smallest extent, and that with great difficulty. In the simile used in <reference osisRef="Amos.3.12">Amo 3:12</reference> there is a slight want of proportion in the two halves, the object of the deliverance being thrown into the background in the second clause by the passive construction, and only indicated in the verb, to deliver themselves, i.e., to save their life. “A pair of shin-bones and a piece (בּדל ἁταξ λεγ.), i.e., a lappet, of the earth,” are most insignificant remnants. The grandees of Samaria, of whom only a few were to escape with their life, are depicted by Amos as those who sit on costly divans, without the least anxiety. פּאת מטּה, the corner of the divan, the most convenient for repose. According to <reference osisRef="Amos.6.4">Amo 6:4</reference>, these divans were ornamented with ivory, and according to the verse before us, they were ornamented with costly stuffs. דּמשׂק comes from דמּשׂק, Damascus, and signifies <hi type="italic">damask</hi>, an artistically woven material (see Ges. <hi type="italic">Thes.</hi> p. 346). This brings the visitation of God to an end. Even the altars and palaces are to be laid in ruins, and consequently Samaria will be destroyed.
entries.1dbfa717b098c0902a813c64bb027ce0c0e448aa: <reference osisRef="Amos.3.13-Amos.3.15">Amo 3:13-15</reference> <div eID="gen16373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16374" type="x-p"/> This feature in the threat is brought out into peculiar prominence by a fresh introduction.
